note_n_minus_3: Q36/Q38/Q39 have an empty relevant set (recall undefined), so they are excluded from all retrieval metrics, leaving n=42. All retrievers score 0.93-0.98 on hit_rate@5 on this corpus, so MRR / nDCG@10 are the discriminating metrics.

chunking.a1_note: fixed-800 is worst on 4 of 5 quality columns (hit_rate@1, recall@5, mrr, ndcg@10) but is actually BEST on hit_rate@5 (0.9524 vs 0.9286 for sliding/recursive) -- that column doesn't discriminate the same failure mode.
chunking.a2_note: hit_rate@1, recall@5, mrr and ndcg@10 fall monotonically 400->800->1600. hit_rate@5 is flat between 400 and 800 (0.9762 -> 0.9762) and only drops at 1600 (0.9524) -- not strictly monotonic across all five columns.

a4_chunking_failure.question: Does Aurora cover treatment in Singapore, and up to what limit?
a4_chunking_failure.chunk_that_should_have_matched: exclusions::m0 - '[Permanent Exclusions] The following are never payable under any Aurora indemnity plan, at any sum insured, regardless of waiting periods served.'
a4_chunking_failure.mechanism: Chaining + partial-grounding failure, not primarily chunk-size. The expected chunk (exclusions::m0) is a generic permanence clause with no Singapore/international-treatment/limit language -- verified against the logged chunk text, which contains no such mention. The gold answer needs exclusions + plans-overview combined, but no chunk found in the corpus states a concrete Singapore/international treatment limit; that figure appears to live in a source (e.g. a Platinum international-benefit addendum) not present in the 30-document corpus. No chunking strategy at any size would fix this: the missing information was never in the corpus.

retrieval.finding_hybrid_loses: dense (ndcg@10 0.8527) beats hybrid (0.7949) by 0.058 on this corpus, reversing T4's default advice: our embedding model already handles the exact identifiers BM25 usually rescues, so fusing a weaker retriever drags down more good rankings than it rescues.

rerank.ndcg_column_note: The harness reports ndcg@10 (not ndcg@5 as the README's C3 table header suggests), computed over the reranked top-5 candidates -- so these ndcg@10 figures are not directly comparable to the larger-pool ndcg@10 figures in the chunking/retrieval sections.

c2_cost.parallelisation: ParallelLLMReranker (16 workers, per labs/lab3/search.py) replaces aip's sequential 30-call-per-query loop. Only the 30 calls within a single query's rerank are parallelised across the 16-worker pool (2 sequential rounds of <=16 calls each), so full sequential execution of the same 1260 calls would take roughly 16x longer, not 30x -- the 30x figure would only apply if a single query's 30 calls ran one at a time with zero parallelism assumed at the wrong granularity.

c3_decision.interactive_search_box: no-rerank dense (p95 4.6ms, $0). No reranker is worth its latency or cost below a hard quality gate; if a rank-sensitive consumer forces a reranker, cross-encoder at 852ms is the only defensible choice.
c3_decision.overnight_batch: llm-rerank (best mrr 0.9048 and hit_rate@1 0.8571); latency is irrelevant overnight and the $0.371/1k amortizes.

rerank.note_cross_encoder_hurts: Cross-encoder (trained on web search) is out-of-domain for insurance-policy prose: it lowers mrr 0.8800->0.8619 and ndcg@10 0.8685->0.8174. The LLM reranker is the only one that improves mrr (0.9048) and hit_rate@1 (0.8571).
rerank.note_warm_cache: The rerank section in lab3_output.txt was last re-run on a warm cache (llm p95 55.6ms, cost $0 are artifacts). Deployment numbers above are from the first uncached run.

index.crossover_note: HNSW first beats exact between 2335 and 7235 chunks (crossover measured at real+1000). At ~235 chunks HNSW is ~2x slower: graph traversal + Python call overhead lose to a single BLAS matmul; HNSW's O(log n) wins once exact O(n*d) grows. Corpus scale was capped at 1000 filler docs (7235 chunks) because the larger 4000-doc filler embedding was not run to completion.

d3_metadata_filter_q29_31.status: chunk.meta['status'] = 'archived' if 'ARCHIVED' in doc_id else 'current'; filtered search where={'status': 'current'}

index.d3_insight: The Q29/Q30/Q31 fix was metadata filtering, not a retriever change: when retrieval quality is poor, look at data hygiene/curation before touching the retriever.

final_recommendation.config: markdown-aware chunking at 400 chars + exact dense retrieval (no reranker for interactive use)
final_recommendation.greedy_sweep_limitation: One axis at a time fixes the winner before moving on, so interactions are missed (e.g. the reranker that is optimal for a different chunking/size, or a size that is optimal for hybrid). A joint search would need a budget we deliberately did not spend.
final_recommendation.surprise: Hybrid retrieval (dense+BM25 via RRF) lost to dense alone (ndcg@10 0.7949 vs 0.8527), reversing the general advice that hybrid is usually the strongest single improvement -- our embedding model already handles the exact identifiers BM25 typically rescues.
